title: name/value pairs and form data
learningObjectives: Explain name/value pairs and form data and build forms with appropriate native HTML behaviour.

understand.concept: HTML forms submit data as name/value pairs. A control's name identifies its field and its value supplies the submitted data. Repeated names are valid for groups such as checkboxes, and FormData can represent multiple values for the same name.
understand.whyItMatters: The submitted payload is not simply a copy of everything visible in the form. Controls may be excluded based on name, disabled state, checked state, and form rules. Server code must validate all received data.
understand.analogy: A name/value pair is like a labelled entry in a form: the label identifies what the value means.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is simplified; actual form submission and validation follow HTML algorithms and browser behaviour.

explain.narrative: The two checked topic boxes produce two entries with the same name and different values.

examples.explanation: The two checked topic boxes produce two entries with the same name and different values.
examples.expectedOutput: A browser-rendered form demonstrating the HTML form behaviour described.

practise.guidedTask: Add a radio group and multiple checkboxes. Inspect FormData entries and explain repeated names.
practise.independentTask: Build an accessible form using appropriate input types, names, labels, and constraints. Inspect the submitted FormData and explain which controls are successful.
hints: Give every user-facing control a visible label.
Do not trust hidden fields or client-side validation for security.
Test keyboard and mobile input behaviour.

questions.prompt: Can multiple successful controls submit the same name?
questions.explanation: Repeated names are valid and common for checkbox groups and other collections.

questions.prompt: What is a good form-design principle?
options: Use semantic controls, visible labels, and server-side validation
questions.answer: Use semantic controls, visible labels, and server-side validation
questions.explanation: Accessible forms use appropriate controls and labels, while security validation belongs on the server.
